newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-Russian crew struggle to keep Mir operational.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Russian crew struggle to keep Mir operational.

text.p: A U.S.-Russian crew is struggling to keep the increasingly decrepit Mir space station habitable, NASA astronaut Jerry Linenger said from space on Friday.
The 11-year-old space station has run into many problems in the past few months, including a fire and the loss of its main oxygen generators. Most recently a cooling system developed leaks.
"It gets very complex very quickly," said Linenger, who has been aboard Mir since January. "We need to fix our problems."

The loss of cooling sent temperatures and humidity aboard the station soaring, knocking out a device for removing carbon dioxide from the air. Fumes from leaking coolant were giving the crew breathing problems.

NASA officials said recently they would review safety aboard Mir before sending any more astronauts to live there. Linenger said the future of the joint U.S.-Russian programme depended on the success of repair work currently under way.
"We need to look closely at the result of the repairs and make sure we have a good environment for those that follow," Linenger said.
British-born astronaut Michael Foale is due to replace Linenger in May, and two more Americans were due to spend time on Mir.
Frank Culbertson, who heads NASA's shuttle-Mir programme, said he was discussing the future of the venture with Russian space authorities.
"I'm optimistic that we will be able to continue with the programme," he said. "The bottom line is we need to have fail-safe systems in all the life-critical systems."
The arrival of an unmanned Progress resupply ship brought repair gear to the station on Tuesday, allowing the crew to plug one leak in the cooling system. They were still searching for another leak.
Linenger said they were wearing breathing masks during repair work to avoid taking in the toxic ethylene glycol coolant.
The system for removing carbon dioxide was restarted on Thursday, although it was still not being cooled properly.
"I think it's kind of a wait-and-see to see how it holds up without getting the adequate cooling," Linenger said. "The carbon dioxide levels have been a concern."

Repairs on Thursday to an oxygen generator were unsuccessful, but the cosmonauts hoped to get it working soon by taking parts from another device. The next shuttle to visit Mir will deliver a replacement oxygen generator.

Twice in the past two months Linenger was ready to abandon ship, he said. The crew prepared to evacuate when fire broke out aboard the station on Feb. 23 and later when they feared an out-of-control unmanned resupply ship could collide with the station.
Linenger, who has been in space for 89 days, was due to end his tour of duty aboard Mir in May when the space shuttle Atlantis arrives to pick him up.
"It will always be nice to see Atlantis," he said.
